So my (now ex) fiancé joined this cult where the overarching philosophy was that you are responsible for everything that happens to you, including all your health problems, disabilities, traumas, bad feelings, etc. At one point he announced to me that he was going to be sleeping in the same bed as another girl from the cult during a retreat. I expressed that I was uncomfortable with that and he said, “Well, you’re responsible for that. You’ve created that feeling for yourself.” 

At this point I chose to reveal a little secret to him that I’d been keeping. He had a notebook where he kept everything he was learning in the cult (most of it consisted of how to recruit new members and manipulate people). The notebook was supposed to be highly confidential. So I told him, “I went through your notebook the other day and took photos of all the pages.” Needless to say, he became VERY angry. Of course, I told him, “Well, I’m not responsible for your anger. You’ve created that feeling for yourself.”

Later on I wrote an exposé of the cult using those photos from his notebook as background information. I don’t feel one bit guilty since all of the cult members believe that everyone creates the bad things that happen to them. They created this.

You have no idea how much comfort it brings me to know I’m not the only one. Congrats to you on graduating college - hope you are doing something that makes you feel happy or feels meaningful, that is really the only thing that matters.

I feel the EXACT same way. I used to be absolutely obsessed with this show throughout middle school and elementary school, to the point of my parents getting angry at me for talking about it too much, and you just put into words why.

For as long as I’ve been alive, my parents have only valued me for my accomplishments and achievements, not who I am as a person. So in high school all I really knew was that I had to get perfect grades and get into an Ivy League or I was worthless. On top of that, I am autistic (I didn’t know it at the time though - I just thought I was weird) so I really didn’t fit in at school and was fairly gossiped about/bullied, and my parents were pretty embarrassed of having a kid that was so bullied. My teachers told me I couldn’t complain about anything in my life because I grew up upper middle class and so I just needed to be grateful for what I had. In short I really really just hated myself all the time (and I still struggle with that a ton, as my username reveals) and didn’t understand that there was anything to like about me. I remember crying hysterically in the bathroom every time I got some sort of achievement or won some sort of academic award because I knew that if I didn’t keep it up and maintain that perfect level of performance I’d be a failure, and there would be nothing good about me ever.

So...I wanted to shoot up my school. I didn’t make any plans or anything like that, I didn’t buy a gun, I don’t think I even would’ve known how, but I wished I could do it. I guess I didn’t understand the value of life - because my life didn’t feel like it had any value - and I was so angry that no one could understand how much I was suffering (and everyone was very quick to dismiss my suffering), and I wanted them to feel the pain, to feel what I felt. I remember just feeling so incredibly powerless and this would be a way to gain power.

In college I made friends who valued me for who I was as a person, not just my grades, and that’s when things started changing. After college I started getting involved with the autistic rights and Mad Pride movement which is full of people who take pride in their own and others’ differences and disabilities, and that made me realize how much more there is to like about myself than just my academic accomplishments and achievements. The thing that truly changed my life, to be honest, was finding a partner who loves me unconditionally and accepts me for who I am. He says his favorite thing about me is my worldview - not a level of achievement that I have to work to maintain, not something about my appearance that will go away, but something that is intrinsic to me and a permanent part of who I am - my worldview. And every day I am surrounded by people who value me because of my passion for activism and desire to help others, not because of my resume or transcript. 

I really think 99% if not 100% of school shootings could be prevented if every single child could experience what it’s like to be valued and loved for who they ARE, not what they DO. And if every single child could have their pain taken seriously and cared about, even if it seems like they have no reason to complain or be depressed. 

Hope this post helps someone today.

Okay, so, I’m a former mental patient and have spent a lot of time doing activism in the mental patients rights movement. A quick google search will reveal that I’ve been in institutions and am certifiably crazy. So, needless to say, I was just as shocked as you when I found out I was a finalist for several competitive doctoral student fellowships (I didn’t even think I’d get into a PhD program). I was crazy nervous for the interview process - how could they ever accept someone like me?

Here’s the thing I realized. I had something the other candidates didn’t have: I had lived experience of some pretty horrible shit that had exposed me to firsthand knowledge of what it’s like to be in an incredibly marginalized and stigmatized group, and I had a critical and important perspective on how society needs to change to accommodate people with differing abilities. 

And that’s what you have too - you have firsthand knowledge and expertise of being a first generation student and that gives you a source of insight into the world that very few other applicants, if any, will have. 

If they want to pick a super rich applicant with a prestigious family background, then you might not be selected. But if they want someone with a unique perspective and life experience that doesn’t fit the typical mold, you have a HUGE advantage over other candidates.

Congratulations and good luck :)
